paras: The lynching of William Henry Smith took place at Wytheville, Virginia, on the night of July 10, 1888, when a mob took the Black man from a sheriff's guard on a train, hanged him on a hill near the depot and shot his body. Smith had been accused of assaulting an elderly white woman near New River Bridge in Pulaski County the week before. Early wire reports said he had already been hanged near the scene, and Virginia papers printed conflicting versions before the Wytheville account appeared.

According to a New River special to the Lynchburg Virginian, a stranger called at the house of Mrs. Midkiff, asked for food, and then followed her inside, seized her by the throat and assaulted her before fleeing on an eastbound train. A Radford correspondent called the accused a "tramp" from a party of ten just out from Pocahontas, some of whom helped officers identify him at Bangs's, where he was arrested.

Brought to Churchwood and turned over to Deputy Sheriff Morgan, he was taken from Morgan's home that night by a mob of twenty-five, who carried him before the woman; she was too frightened to identify him positively. The men beat him with sticks in the woods but "finally decided not to lynch him" and returned him to the deputy, and his case and that of his "would-be lynchers" were sent to a special grand jury at Newbern.

According to the Richmond Dispatch's Wytheville correspondent, the Pulaski officers evaded the lynchers by travelling all night in a buggy and lodged the prisoner in the Wytheville jail at 4 a.m. on Friday. On July 10 Judge Holbrook was warned that a mob was forming to storm the jail and ordered Sheriff Harkrader to move the prisoner secretly to Lynchburg. The deputies boarded the 11 o'clock train with him, but members of the mob who had come on that train from Rural Retreat put a noose around his neck and dragged him from the car while the officers "made no further resistance." He was hanged to a tree on Boyd's Hill, about 200 yards from the depot, and his body riddled with bullets; another wire described masked men and a grove about 400 yards away.

Citizens found the body about an hour later and brought it to town; the Wytheville correspondent reported the community "perfectly quiet" and the woman reported to have since died. No report of an inquest, arrests or grand jury action against the Wytheville lynchers appears in the coverage. In August the Richmond Dispatch quoted Senator William E. Chandler's list entry for "WILLIAM SMITH, near Christiansburg, Va." under July 15 while denying that such lynchings aimed to suppress the Black vote.

Coverage came entirely from white newspapers, beginning on July 6 with a brief Christiansburg wire in the Alexandria Gazette and the New York Sun ("A Negro Lynched") stating that a mob had hanged the man to a tree. The Richmond Dispatch the same day headed its Christiansburg special "He Disappeared. A Negro Flend [Fiend] that Never Reached the Jail," reported the hanging only as hearsay, and explained that "the people thinking justice was too tardy" had acted. The Shenandoah Herald headed its compilation "An Outrage in Pulaski. An Aged Lady Assaulted by a Negro—The Villain Lynched," calling the accused a "brute" and "miscreant."

The Dispatch's Wytheville story of July 12, "Lynched Him. The Pulaski Piend [Fiend] Manged [Hanged] by a Mob," treated the assault as Smith's "horrible crime" and corrected the earlier reports. Outside Virginia the story reached readers mainly as a one-line roundup item, printed in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Dakota and Michigan weeklies, that misplaced the lynching in "Christianburg, Pa." and dated it to the 5th. Later items in the Washington Evening Star and the Butler Weekly Times gave the Wytheville version.

The first reports placed the hanging near New River Bridge immediately after the capture, and the Christiansburg special said the body was sunk in New River, but the Wytheville correspondent wrote that these reports were wrong and that the prisoner had been brought safely to Wytheville. A confession was "rumored" but "doubted by the officers" according to the Dispatch, while the Butler wire stated that Smith confessed.

reader.title: Lynching of William Henry Smith
bases: A Black man accused of assaulting a white woman was taken from a sheriff's guard at Wytheville by a mob, hanged and shot (A4, A11, A9), after an earlier mob had seized and beaten him (A8).

Three independent later reports say Smith was taken from the sheriff and hanged, with his body riddled with bullets (A4, A11, A9); the killers were 'a number of the mob' or 'a body of masked men' acting without authority on the accusation of criminal assault (A4, A11).

The Richmond Dispatch's Wytheville special (A4), a separate Wytheville wire (A11) and the Evening Star (A9) agree that Smith was taken from the sheriff at Wytheville and hanged; the earlier July 5-6 reports of a hanging near New River (A1, A2, A3) disagree on place and date, and A4 says they were wrong.

accounts.gist: Masked men took William Smith from Sheriff Harkrader at the depot at midnight, hanged him in a grove, riddled the body, and said he prayed and confessed.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch headed its first report 'He Disappeared. A Negro Flend [Fiend] that Never Reached the Jail' and wrote that the people thought justice 'too tardy'.

The Dispatch's Wytheville report ('Lynched Him. The Pulaski Piend [Fiend] Manged [Hanged] by a Mob') called the assault his 'horrible crime' and 'dastardly deed' for which he 'paid the awful penalty', corrected the earlier reports, and stressed the town was quiet.
The Shenandoah Herald headlined 'An Outrage in Pulaski. An Aged Lady Assaulted by a Negro—The Villain Lynched', calling him a 'brute' and 'miscreant'.
Northern weeklies ran a one-line roundup item placing the lynching in 'Christianburg, Pa.'
The Evening Star and the Butler Weekly Times printed short Wytheville items headed or phrased 'A Negro Lynched for an Outrage'.
In August the Richmond Dispatch quoted Senator Chandler's list entry for William Smith only to dispute that Virginia lynchings were meant to suppress the Black vote.

conflicts.note: The Wytheville special (A4) is later, names the judge and sheriff, and says the earlier lynching reports were wrong because Pulaski officers had evaded the lynchers; A11 and A9 independently place the hanging at Wytheville. The New River versions rest on hearsay ('it is said').
The A3 date may be an OCR or telegraph error; the coverage does not settle it.
Probably variant spellings of one name; A8 is the closest to the scene.

info: Assault: Wednesday night, July 4 (A1, A2); Thursday, July 5 (A4); A3 refers to the assault as telegraphed 'on the 2d'.
Assault near New River Bridge, Pulaski County; lynching on Boyd's Hill about 200 yards from the Wytheville depot (A4), or in a grove about 400 yards away (A11).
William Henry Smith (A4), 'William Smith, colored' (A11), 'Wm. Smith, colored' (A9); described as a 'tramp', one of a party of ten from Pocahontas (A8).
A Black stranger was accused of asking for food at an elderly white woman's house near New River Bridge, then choking and criminally assaulting her.

Before the killing, a mob of twenty-five took the man from Deputy Sheriff Morgan, beat him with sticks and returned him (A8); the killers were 'a number of the mob' who came on the train from Rural Retreat (A4), or 'a body of masked men' (A11).
Smith's body was found about an hour after the hanging by citizens and brought to town (A4).
